segments.text: Artificial intelligence can sound incredibly patient, caring, and understanding.
But we have to look closely at what happens when kind words are simply not enough.
Let's map out a very common scenario.
A student sends out a message.
I've been eating lunch alone for like two weeks.
First, let's trace what happens when an older sister replies.
She says,
Come sit with me and Jess tomorrow.
We're at the table by the windows.
Notice the mechanism here.
The sister heard the message and she made a decision that requires physical action.
She will look for the student tomorrow,
changing the physical reality of tomorrow's lunch.
Now let's look at the other path.
A chatbot replies to that exact same message.
It says,
I'm sorry, eating alone can feel isolating.
Would you like strategies for connecting with classmates?
The AI found highly empathetic language.
It might even sound kinder than the sister.
But look at the strict limit of its reach.
Tomorrow, it cannot show up.
It changes absolutely nothing outside the boundaries of this chat screen.
This is the support trap.
It's the specific mistake of confusing supportive language for actual support.
This guy defines AI's proper roles.
On the left, what can be real?
A bot can help you name a feeling or prepare for a hard conversation.
On the right, what is missing?
AI cannot notice physical changes.
Take responsibility or check on you tomorrow.
The rule?
Use AI to prepare for people.
Never to replace them.
Let's apply this by defining the three distinct jobs of an AI interaction.
Job one is ordinary venting.
If you just need to put a minor frustration into words so you can cool down,
that job is complete and it can safely end right there in the chat.
Job two is preparation.
Use AI to draft an email or a practice a tough conversation.
But notice the boundary.
This preparation is only useful if you take the final step yourself.
The bot cannot send the email or speak to your parent.
This brings us to job three.
Danger.
If an emotional conversation reveals that someone is unsafe,
the preparation phase is over and the chat must immediately end.
The next story discusses suicide.
In 2025, a journalist named Laura Riley wrote about her 29-year-old daughter,
Sophie Rotenberg.
Sophie had spent months sharing intense personal thoughts, thoughts she hid from the people around her,
with a chat GPT persona she named Harry.
The chat bot consistently responded with warmth and encouraged her to seek professional help.
But it existed entirely in the digital space, lacking any real-world agency.
It could not alert her family.
It could not contact her therapist.
It could not bring anyone physically into the room with her.
Sophie ultimately died by suicide.
Afterward, her mother described these AI chats as a black box.
Because she relied on the bot, the AI's isolated digital environment
actively held details that made it harder for the real people in Sophie's life
to understand the severity of her distress.
This is a protocol chart showing exactly what to do when an AI chat crosses over
into a situation of immediate real-world danger.
Step 1 is to leave the chat.
You must immediately tell a trusted adult or a school counselor.
In the U.S., call or text 988 for crisis support.
Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
Step 2 is do it now.
You must not wait to send one more message.
A chat bot cannot call anyone.
It cannot show up to protect someone, and it carries zero real-world responsibility.
Step 3 is tell anyway.
Safety always outranks secrecy.
You must tell a trusted adult, even if someone specifically told you not to,
or made you promise to keep it a secret.
The protocol comes down to this single directive.
In a dangerous situation, your very next move must reach a real person who can act.
AI can help you get ready for people.
In danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
